title: Bats by the numbers
text:
Bats come in very different sizes. Below are approximate values for seven species.


Show the code
species = [
    "Kitti's hog-nosed bat",
    "Common pipistrelle",
    "Brandt's bat",
    "Mexican free-tailed bat",
    "Common vampire bat",
    "Egyptian fruit bat",
    "Large flying fox",
]
mass_g = [2, 5, 7, 12, 35, 140, 1000]       # body mass in grams
wingspan_cm = [16, 22, 23, 32, 38, 60, 150]  # wingspan in centimetres

for name, m, w in zip(species, mass_g, wingspan_cm):
    print(f"{name:<25} {m:>5} g   {w:>4} cm")


Kitti's hog-nosed bat         2 g     16 cm
Common pipistrelle            5 g     22 cm
Brandt's bat                  7 g     23 cm
Mexican free-tailed bat      12 g     32 cm
Common vampire bat           35 g     38 cm
Egyptian fruit bat          140 g     60 cm
Large flying fox           1000 g    150 cm


The heaviest bat in this list weighs about 500 times as much as the lightest. Figure 1 shows how wingspan grows with body mass.








Figure 1: Wingspan against body mass for seven bat species (approximate values). Mass is on a logarithmic scale.

title: Bats by the numbers
text:
Seeing with sound
Many bats find insects by echolocation: they shout and listen for the echo. The calls are mostly between 20 and 200 kHz, too high for humans to hear (we stop at about 20 kHz).
How small an object a bat can detect depends on the wavelength of its call:
\[
\lambda = \frac{v}{f}
\]
where \(v \approx 343\) m/s is the speed of sound in air and \(f\) is the call frequency.

speed_of_sound = 343  # m/s

for f_khz in [20, 50, 100, 200]:
    wavelength_mm = speed_of_sound / (f_khz * 1000) * 1000
    print(f"{f_khz:>3} kHz  ->  wavelength {wavelength_mm:.1f} mm")

 20 kHz  ->  wavelength 17.1 mm
 50 kHz  ->  wavelength 6.9 mm
100 kHz  ->  wavelength 3.4 mm
200 kHz  ->  wavelength 1.7 mm


At higher frequencies the wavelength is only a few millimetres, about the size of a mosquito. That’s why insect-hunting bats use such high calls.
This block is shown but not run, because it only explains the idea:


Show the code
# A bat hears its echo after time t, so the distance to the insect is
distance = speed_of_sound * t / 2

title: Bats: the basics
text:
Bats are mammals, and they are the only mammals that can truly fly. Gliders such as flying squirrels can only fall with style.
Their scientific name, Chiroptera, comes from Greek and means “hand wing”. A bat’s wing is a hand: long finger bones with a thin skin stretched between them.

title: Bats: the basics
text:
Bats are mammals, and they are the only mammals that can truly fly. Gliders such as flying squirrels can only fall with style.
Their scientific name, Chiroptera, comes from Greek and means “hand wing”. A bat’s wing is a hand: long finger bones with a thin skin stretched between them.

title: Bats: the basics
text:
How many are there?
There are more than 1,400 bat species. That makes bats the second-largest group of mammals, after rodents.


Roughly 22% of all mammal species are bats.

title: Bats: the basics
text:
Five fun facts

The smallest bat, Kitti’s hog-nosed bat, weighs about 2 grams, less than a sugar cube.
The largest, the flying foxes, have wings spanning up to about 1.5 metres.
A Brandt’s bat lived for over 40 years in the wild. For a 7-gram animal, that is extraordinary.
Bracken Cave in Texas is home to around 15 million bats each summer, the largest known bat colony.
Bats help make tequila: they pollinate the agave plant.

title: Bats: the basics
text:
Myth or fact?

“Bats are blind”“Bats drink blood”“Bats are pest controllers”


Myth. All bats can see. Many species also use echolocation to hunt in the dark, and fruit bats have excellent eyesight.


Mostly myth. Only 3 of over 1,400 species feed on blood, all in Central and South America. Most bats eat insects or fruit.


Fact. A single small bat can eat hundreds of insects in one night, including mosquitoes and crop pests.
